source.title: Interpreting learned search: finding a transition model and value function in an RNN that plays Sokoban
source.authors: Mohammad Taufeeque; A. D. Tucker; Adam Gleave; Adrià Garriga-Alonso

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. The title in the supplied metadata differs from the paper title shown in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests internal look-ahead and causal plan representations in a Sokoban RNN using channel analyses and interventions, rather than the language-model methods in the original sources.
record.gate_note: The study reports AUC-based prediction of future moves, interventions on path channels, and interventions on plan-extension mechanisms. Its cited prior probe results are not recorded as study results. The weight-steering results on larger boards are omitted because they demonstrate a deliberately modified network solving larger levels, not spontaneous look-ahead in the trained network.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own results on internal look-ahead in a Sokoban convolutional RNN. These include AUC of path channels for moves up to about 50 steps ahead, cache ablations of plan storage, and causal interventions on plan channels and plan-building kernels. Sokoban is a setting V5 names, and the results bear on V6's claim that plans are shallow or incidental. It is a new setting and architecture relative to the LM originals, so T3 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that the DRC(3,3) stores its intended path in path channels. Encoder kernels initialize these channels, forward/backward plan-extension kernels extend them bidirectionally, and a winner-takes-all mechanism stabilizes them. Negative obstacle activations enable backtracking. They read these as parts of a learned transition model and value function. They also claim the network is a model organism of a mesa-optimizer, answering affirmatively that such optimizers exist.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes a convolutional recurrent reinforcement-learning agent using channel inspection, AUC measurements, kernel analysis, and causal interventions. It does not use rhyme-generation prompts, language-model hidden-state probes, or language-model attribution graphs.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary between path and non-path channel ablations, random and identified path-channel subsets, short- and long-term channels, and box- versus agent-movement channels. The agent-movement intervention score depends on whether the agent is pushing a box; the paper did not filter the tested transitions for this.
record.problems: The detailed analysis centers on one DRC(3, 3) seed, although the authors report structural replication on four additional seeds. The paper states it does not fully reverse-engineer the network and describes unresolved, sometimes apparently irrelevant plan-selection heuristics. Several AUC results are presented graphically without exact values in the text. The findings concern a Sokoban reinforcement-learning RNN, not a language model.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. Cited probe results from earlier papers and weight-steering results on larger boards were not included.

untested.parts: Multi-step reasoning in LMs, chess, and non-DRC architectures. The authors note that transformers or ResNets might learn different algorithms.
Whether plans in language models are shallow or incidental. Only the Sokoban DRC is tested.
Not tested: no rhyming verse or language model.
Not tested: no language-model hidden-state token prediction.
Not tested: no comparison of pre-caching with next-token side effects in a language model.
Not tested: no open-weight language models.

missing.what: In the unmodified network, plan activations decay and cannot extend beyond 10–15 squares on a 40x40 backtrack level. The network fails zig-zag levels with n>15. This is a depth limit on spontaneous planning outside the training size, separate from the weight-steering results the record excluded.

Long-term channels hold a second planned push at the same square well before the first push, and transfer it to short-term channels after the first push (Figure 5, Appendix H). This is qualitative evidence of multi-horizon plan storage.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed to T3: Sokoban is a new setting relative to the LM originals and is explicitly named in V5. The rows linked to V6 were trimmed to the depth and causal measures. Channel counts and next-action readouts were unlinked or limited to V5. The analysis rests on one seed in detail; the authors say they do not fully reverse-engineer the network and note seemingly arbitrary plan-selection heuristics.

versions.untested_parts: Rhyming verse, candidate rhyme words, and interventions that change an intermediate line to fit a different ending.
The study examines future Sokoban moves, not future token decodability from a language model hidden state.

The system is an RNN trained with model-free reinforcement learning, not a next-token-prediction language model; the study does not compare future-useful features with next-token side effects in that setting.
No open-weight language models or rhyme-planning mechanisms are tested.
The study tests a Sokoban RNN only. It does not test multi-step reasoning or chess, nor other architectures.
The study tests planning depth and causal plan mechanisms in Sokoban, not whether language-model plans are shallow or incidental.

relationships.condition: DRC(3,3) trained on Boxoban 10x10 levels, main seed plus four replication seeds
relationships.reason: Path channels predict box and agent moves beyond 10 steps. Ablating them cuts solve rate 57.6% (41.3% for a random 37-channel subset of path channels). Box-plan interventions redirect actions in 86–88% of transitions. Kernel ablations and obstacle-activation interventions change plan selection and backtracking. The structure recurs across seeds (R1, R3–R7, R11, R12, R14–R16, R18–R22).
relationships.display_finding: Path channels predicted box and agent moves beyond 10 steps; ablating them reduced solve rate by 57.6%, versus 41.3% for a random 37-channel subset of path channels; box-plan interventions redirected actions in 86–88% of transitions, other interventions changed plan selection and backtracking, and the structure recurred across the main seed and four replication seeds.

relationships.condition: Agent-movement channels; short-term negative activations; levels larger than training size
relationships.reason: Agent-movement interventions succeed in only 53.2% of transitions, and short-term backtracking interventions in 48.9% (R13, R17). The text (Appendix L, Fig. 22) also says the original network's plan decays beyond 10–15 squares on 40x40 levels; no row records this.
relationships.display_finding: Agent-movement interventions succeeded in 53.2% of transitions and short-term backtracking interventions in 48.9%; on 40×40 levels, the original network's plan decayed beyond 10–15 squares.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Agent-movement channels; short-term negative activations; levels larger than training size
source_check.reason: Intervention success is incomplete, and unsteered planning fails on larger levels. Agent-only scores include box-pushing transitions; short-term negative activations also implement inhibition and deadlock heuristics, so their lower success rates do not alone establish absent planning.

relationships.condition: Sokoban DRC(3,3) on in-distribution Boxoban levels
relationships.reason: Long-term channels predict moves roughly 10–50 steps ahead (R5, R7). Removing stored plan information cuts solve rate 57.6% (R1). Edits to plan channels and obstacle activations steer actions and backtracking (R11, R12, R15, R16). So these plans are deep and causal, not local next-step features.
relationships.display_finding: Long-term channels predicted moves roughly 10–50 steps ahead, removing stored plans cut solve rate by 57.6%, and plan-channel and obstacle edits steered actions and backtracking.
